target_customer: College newspapers and other newsroom or group-writing teams (15 college papers in beta in 2007)
problem: Groups writing and editing one document pass Word files around by email with no version control or task tracking.
business_model: Web app for newsrooms and writing groups, pricing not found; the TechCrunch launch piece framed enterprise newspaper systems at over 100,000 USD in licenses as the alternative
product_category: Collaborative writing and editing web app

founders.name: Phil Kast
founders.background_notes: Only founder named on the YC page. No background found in sources opened.

competitors.name: Managing Editor (maned.com)
competitors.what: Enterprise content management software for newspapers
competitors.traction_then: Not stated; article says such licenses can cost upwards of 100,000 USD

technical_complexity.rationale: Document editor built on the Dojo Ajax toolkit with uploads, version diffs, comments, tasks and publishing to WordPress or Typepad. Standard web engineering for a two person team in 2007; no complex WYSIWYG layout.

defensibility.rationale: Features were copyable and Google bought Writely in 2006, so a free collaborative editor from a large company already existed. Newsroom workflow labels were the only differentiation.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Google Docs became the free default for group editing. The only retrospective found says the product failed partly because organizations stayed on Word.

market_need_then: Two founders wrote for the Stanford Daily and Binghamton Pipedream and felt the pain of editing articles by email; 15 college newspapers in the US and Canada were in beta by April 2007.

branding.domain_note: writewith.com was the product domain; the domain did not resolve from this session.

identity.voice_and_tone: plain and functional per the TechCrunch launch coverage

brand_strength.rationale: No brand coverage found beyond one TechCrunch launch post; the name is a plain verb phrase that is hard to search for.

outcome_analysis: WriteWith launched in April 2007 as a collaborative writing tool for college newspapers and was listed Inactive by YC with no public shutdown date. A 2013 TechCrunch article quotes Eric Eldon saying it failed for many reasons, a main one being that too many organizations were stubbornly stuck on Word. Google Docs, born from Writely, already offered free group editing, so the wedge was thin.
notes: Company website did not resolve (DNS failure). The 2013 TechCrunch article was summarized by a fetch tool as calling WriteWith Eric Eldon's startup, but the wording was ambiguous and the YC page lists only Phil Kast, so Eldon is not recorded as a founder. The TechCrunch launch post says two founders but names neither. Kando (aggregator) lists a YC seed round with no amount or date, so it is not recorded as a round. Status Inactive per the YC directory; no shutdown date or announcement found. Competitor list rests on one article.
